slides.text: When two masked men shoved me into the back of a dusty van, I was terrified. Then they showed me the ransom note they were about to text my husband, Arthur. I taught AP English for thirty-four years, and frankly, my fear vanished beneath a wave of pedagogical disgust. 'You used "your" instead of "you're" twice,' I said through the duct tape, 'and a comma splice in a death threat completely ruins the urgency.'

The taller kidnapper, Kyle, looked deeply hurt. 'I wrote it under a lot of pressure, ma'am.' I sighed, wriggling a hand free, and pulled a red felt-tip pen from my cardigan. For forty-five minutes, we workshopped their prose on the floor of the van. I replaced 'give us the cash or else' with 'failure to remit the stipulated sum by dusk shall result in irreversible marital bereavement.' Kyle actually teared up at the cadence.

When they finally sent the revised message to Arthur, my phone buzzed immediately. Arthur replied: 'Nice try, Brenda. Nobody in this hemisphere uses the subjunctive mood and an Oxford comma except you. Pick up oat milk on your way home.' The kidnappers stared at me in silence, untied my ankles, and dropped me off at Trader Joe's. Kyle still emails me his short stories every Tuesday.
